spans.text: “Importing, exporting, and backing up data” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.

spans.code:
sqlite3 school.db
.mode csv
.import students.csv students
.headers on
.once students_export.csv
SELECT student_id, name FROM students;

-- PostgreSQL psql client:
-- \copy students(name) FROM 'students.csv' CSV HEADER

-- Backups:
-- SQLite: .backup school-backup.db
-- PostgreSQL: pg_dump school > school.sql
-- MySQL: mysqldump school > school.sql

spans.text: The SQLite commands import CSV and export query results; other DBMSs use their own tools.

Loading a table from CSV and exporting results are common for analysis and moving data between systems. In the SQLite shell, `.mode csv` and `.import students.csv students` import a CSV; `.headers on`, `.once result.csv`, and a SELECT can write results to CSV. PostgreSQL's psql `\copy` works with a file on the client machine; MySQL `LOAD DATA` may require server permissions. Check the schema and encoding first, and never concatenate untrusted CSV values into SQL text. Backup tools include SQLite `.backup`, PostgreSQL `pg_dump`, and MySQL `mysqldump`; store backups separately and test restores.

Key line: `sqlite3 school.db`
What it does: The SQLite commands import CSV and export query results; other DBMSs use their own tools.
Why it is used: Test with a few rows first; confirm CSV delimiters, headers, encoding, and how empty values are represented.
If omitted or changed: CSV carries values, not the full schema; recreate types, constraints, and relationships separately.

spans.title: Common mistake
spans.text: Exports can contain personal data; restrict access and regularly test backup restoration.
